The user-visible label of the app, as shown on the home screen and in the app drawer.
The unique identifier for this app on the device. No two apps can share the same package name.
The name of the operating system process the app runs in. By default, it matches the package name.
The unique identifier assigned to this app by the Android system. It determines the app\'s access to system resources and file permissions.
This app declares that it runs under a shared identity with other apps signed by the same key. Apps sharing this identity can access each other\'s data and permissions as if they were one app.
An optional summary provided by the app developer in the manifest.
The human-readable version string displayed to users, such as \"2.5.1\" or \"Beta 3\".
An internal integer that increases with every release. The system uses it to determine whether one version is newer than another.
The lowest Android API level this app supports. Devices running an older version cannot install it.
The API level the app was designed and tested for. It tells the system which compatibility behaviors to apply.

Development tools can inspect and control this app while it runs. This helps during testing, but published apps usually turn it off because anyone with debugging access to the device gets extra access to the app.
Development tools cannot attach to this app using Android\'s normal app-debugging access.
Android may include this app\'s data in backups or move it to another device. The exact data depends on the app\'s backup rules and the Android version.
The app disables Android cloud backup. Device-to-device transfer may still vary by Android version and device manufacturer.
The app\'s general manifest setting allows network connections without encryption. Custom network security rules can override this setting. This does not prove the app sends unencrypted data.
The app\'s general manifest setting disables network connections without encryption. Custom network security rules and some networking libraries can behave differently.
Whether the app is a pre-installed system app or a user-installed app. System apps have elevated privileges and cannot be fully uninstalled.
The package name of the app that performed the installation, such as \"com.android.vending\" for Google Play.
The app that started the installation, such as a browser or file manager for a sideloaded app, or an app store for a store install. This can differ from the installer package above.
The package that provided the APK file, when Android reports it separately from the app that started the installation. Most installs leave this blank.
The date and time this app was first installed on the device.
The date and time of the most recent update to this app.
The approximate date and time this app was last opened by the user.
The file system path where the APK file is stored on the device.
The file system path where the app stores its private data, databases, and shared preferences.
The preferred storage location declared by the developer — internal storage, external storage, or automatic.

The combined size of the installed APK files on disk, excluding app data, caches, and runtime-generated files. Most apps installed from Google Play are split into a base APK plus additional APKs for your device\'s language and screen density; this total covers all of them.
The combined size of the APK, app data, and cached files. Requires usage access permission.
